claims.text: Engineering a heterogeneous gradient microstructure through surface mechanical treatment can concurrently improve strength and ductility.
A typical untreated steel or aluminum alloy can have a homogeneous, coarse-grained, uniform microstructure.
Surface mechanical attrition treatment can create a gradient nanostructured surface layer while retaining a relatively coarse-grained core.
Optimizing treatment duration and intensity can produce a pronounced gradient microstructure.
The resulting gradient microstructure consists of a fine-grained or nanostructured surface coupled to a coarser-grained, ductile interior.
The fine-grained or nanostructured surface layer increases yield strength by hindering dislocation motion.
The coarse-grained, ductile core maintains overall deformation compatibility.
Strain partitioning between the hard surface and soft interior enhances work hardening.
Enhanced work hardening caused by strain partitioning delays necking.
The treated material will exhibit higher yield strength than its untreated homogeneous counterpart.
The treated material will exhibit greater uniform elongation than its untreated homogeneous counterpart.
The concurrent strength–ductility improvement results from synergy between the strengthened gradient surface and the retained ductility of the core.
An untreated homogeneous coarse-grained sample typically has lower strength but acceptable ductility.
The improvement requires a sufficiently thick and well-controlled gradient layer.
The benefits may not occur in materials that respond poorly to surface mechanical treatment or have limited plastic-deformation capacity.
The magnitude of the strength and ductility enhancement depends on treatment parameters and material composition.
